name: 20-20-20 rule / screen breaks

lead: The 20-20-20 rule asks screen users to look at something 20 feet away for 20 seconds every 20 minutes. People follow it to ease dry, strained eyes and the red, tired look that comes with long screen days.

Looking into the distance relaxes close-focus effort, and breaks may encourage blinking, which reviews cite as relevant to dry, strained eyes. Reviews list breaks among digital eye strain management options, and a 2023 study tested the rule directly for strain and dry eye. Appearance effects have not been studied.

paras: Most people set a repeating timer or use a reminder app while working at a screen, glancing out a window or down a hallway during each break. It costs nothing and is used all day.
No harms are documented. Persistent eye symptoms are a matter for an eye-care professional.

angle.text: Regular distance breaks relax close-focus effort and encourage blinking, so screen days leave less dryness and strain and the eyes look less red and tired. The rule has been studied for strain comfort, not eye whiteness.

lead: The 20-20-20 rule is a commonly cited habit for screen users: every 20 minutes, look at something about 20 feet (6 metres) away for 20 seconds. It is promoted as a way to reduce digital eye strain, with tired, dry or red eyes often named among the symptoms.[1][2]

Digital eye strain, also called computer vision syndrome, covers visual and ocular symptoms linked to prolonged device use, such as dry eyes, itching, blurred vision and headache; reported prevalence varies widely between studies.[2][3] A 2023 study specifically tested the 20-20-20 rule's effect on digital eye strain, dry eye and binocular vision.[4]
infobox: Every 20 minutes, look 20 feet away for 20 seconds

paras: Wikipedia describes the rule as commonly cited advice attributed to optometrists, while noting the article gives no specific professional guideline for it.[1] Other suggestions in the same references include blinking regularly, artificial tears for dry eye, and adjusting screen settings and posture.[1][5]

A 2018 review stated that prevalence may be 50% or more among computer users, with symptoms divided between those linked to focusing or binocular vision stress and external ocular surface symptoms.[2] A 2022 comprehensive review reported pre-pandemic prevalence ranging from 5 to 65%, rising with pandemic-era device use.[3] Surveys of children and students during COVID-19 lockdowns reported high rates of symptoms.[6][7]
Clinical reviews of management and a Lifestyle report on the digital environment and the ocular surface discuss breaks, ergonomics and blinking among interventions.[5][8]

A 2023 study in Contact Lens & Anterior Eye examined the effects of breaks on digital eye strain, dry eye and binocular vision by testing the 20-20-20 rule.[4] Reviews of digital eye strain treat breaks as one of several management measures alongside ergonomics and dry-eye care.[2][5] No studies found testing the rule specifically for the cosmetic whiteness of the eyes.
